newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanian sugar industry pins hopes on privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian sugar industry pins hopes on privatisation.

text.p: With most of its production capacity requiring massive renovation and repairs, the future viability of Tanzania's sugar industry hinges on privatisation, a senior sugar executive said on Tuesday.

Sugar Development Corporation General Manager George Mbati told Reuters in an interview, "it is hoped...privatisation will attract both international and local capital badly needed to rehabilitate the mills."
"The (sugar) sector is up for privatisation. All factories are programmed for privatisation effective 1997," he said.
Mbati said total 1996/97 sugar production was forecast at about 100,000 tonnes worth an estimated $45 million or half of Tanzania's through-put production capacity of 200,000 tonnes.
Annual production for 1995/96 season was 120,000 tonnes.
Tanzania's domestic demand is currently running at 280,000 tonnes annually with the deficit imported under the country's liberalised trade regime, Mbati told Reuters.
Despite the deficit, the Corporation was tenaciously holding onto a 10,000 tonne quota for the European Union worth two and half times the import parity price, Mbati said.
Only two of the vast East African country's five sugar mills which produce "plantation white" or raw sugar are currently profitable enterprises, Mbati said.

In a summary of Tanzania's sugar mills, Mbati said two factories at central Kilombero were operating with obsolete and broken equipment, but if repaired could have a combined production capacity of 76,000 tonnes per year.
At Kagera on the shores of Lake Victoria near western Bukoba, a giant mill commissioned in 1982 and capable of 56,000 tonnes per year output was producing a miserly 6,000 tonnes.
Low output at Kagera was due to a problem of cane supply, a problem exacerbated by local growers harvesting "rain-fed cane" in place of irrigated cane.

The African Development Bank (AfDB) funded a study on rehabilitating the mill and a draft study by the U.S.-based company Arkel was almost ready, Mbati said: "Hopefully, we can attract investors to assist in rehabilitating the factory including the irrigation component."
He said the situation was improved at the Mtibwa mill near Dodoma which was operating at 100 percent capacity, producing 34,000 tonnes per year.
"A very prominent feature of this factory is a large outgrowers scheme delivering to the factory approximately 60 percent of the cane throughput," said Mbati.
At northern Moshi, a mill was operating at just over 50 percent capacity producing an annual output of 38,000 tonnes.
The main problems at Moshi stemmed from a dilapidated power house at the mill, transport problems for farmers and a pest known as "White grub", Mbati said.

White grub is a beetle which attacks the roots of the sugar cane plant and is known to effect 20 percent of land under cultivation, some 7,000 hectares. Salinity is another problem faced by growers at Moshi, he said.
Mbati said Tanzania could be a net sugar exporter if sufficient capital was invested into the industry.
"Except for Kagera and Kilombero, the other mills are profitable enterprises," he said.
